title: Air India Mandates Drug Testing for All Pilots After Phuket-Delhi Incident
excerpt: The Tata-owned carrier launched mandatory screening for all group pilots after the captain of a flight that lost 300 feet of altitude tested positive for marijuana.
body:
• Air India has introduced mandatory drug and medication screening for all pilots across the airline group, going beyond existing DGCA regulatory requirements.
  • The initiative follows an August 4 incident where flight AI2379 from Phuket to Delhi experienced a sudden 300-foot altitude loss during cruise, injuring 24 passengers and crew.
  • The pilot-in-command's confirmatory drug test returned positive for marijuana, according to sources cited by Hindustan Times and Livemint.
  • Both pilots have been taken off roster, and the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has classified the occurrence as a "serious incident."

Air India has launched mandatory drug and medication screening for all pilots across its group, a sweeping safety measure that goes beyond existing regulatory requirements. The initiative follows the fallout from an August 4 flight that dropped 300 feet mid-cruise and a subsequent drug test that found the pilot-in-command positive for marijuana.

The Phuket-Delhi Incident

On August 4, Air India flight AI2379, an Airbus A320 carrying 137 passengers and eight crew members from Phuket to Delhi, experienced a sudden loss of approximately 300 feet of altitude during cruise, according to a statement from India's civil aviation ministry. The aircraft stabilized and landed safely in Delhi, but 20 passengers and four crew members suffered injuries, according to reporting by TBS News.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=KgrHqsZc75M

The Directorate General of Civil Aviation classified the occurrence as a "serious incident" and referred it to the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau for a full probe.

Drug Test Results

Under standard post-incident procedures, both pilots underwent psychoactive substance screening after landing. The pilot-in-command's initial screening returned a "not-negative" result, prompting confirmatory laboratory testing, according to a government statement reported by Reuters on August 9.

The confirmatory test came back positive for marijuana, according to two people with knowledge of the development cited by Livemint. Air India and the civil aviation ministry have not officially confirmed the specific substance.

"We are aware that a post-flight screening test was conducted on the pilots in accordance with applicable protocols. However, the results of the test have not been shared with Air India, and we are therefore not in a position to comment on any findings."

— Air India Spokesperson

Both pilots have been taken off the roster pending the investigation. Air India's outgoing CEO Campbell Wilson met officials at the civil aviation ministry and DGCA following the revelations.

The New Testing Regime

According to an internal communication issued to pilots on August 13 and reviewed by Reuters, the expanded testing program covers all Air India group pilots and extends beyond the existing regulatory requirements prescribed by the DGCA, according to reporting by Madhyamam Online.

The airline stated it already complies with DGCA norms, which align with major international aviation standards in Europe and the United States, but chose to implement a comprehensive screening to ensure no prohibited substances or medications are in use across its pilot workforce.

Screening will be compulsory and carried out at multiple touchpoints: during training sessions at the airline's Gurugram Academy, at Flight Briefing Centres after flights, at Air India offices, and at designated locations across operating bases, according to the internal communication reported by LatestLY.

Broader Safety Questions

The incident has raised questions beyond drug use. A preliminary defect report prepared by the pilots suggested the altitude loss was preceded by multiple technical issues, including an autopilot disconnection, according to sources cited by TBS News. Investigators are examining whether the pilots handled the event appropriately, whether weather or mechanical factors contributed, and whether the aircraft sustained damage including possible hydraulic system issues.

It was also revealed that the pilot-in-command had been taking medication for sleep difficulties, according to Madhyamam Online — raising separate questions about medication disclosure protocols for flight crew.

What's Next

Further action against the pilots will depend on the outcome of the AAIB investigation and any additional regulatory findings. The case has renewed calls for stricter oversight of pilot fitness standards in Indian aviation, where rapid fleet expansion across carriers including Air India, IndiGo, and Akasa has increased demand for qualified flight crew. The airline has said it will continue to cooperate with relevant authorities.
